question.problem: The polar curve $r=k\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ where $k$ is a constant, passes through the point $A$ with Cartesian coordinates $(-\frac{9}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}).$ What is the value of $k?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the polar coordinates of the point $A.$ The distance from $A$ to the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{9}{2})}^{2}+{(-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{81}{4}+\frac{27}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{27} \\  & =3\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $A$ lies in the third quadrant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}}{-\frac{9}{2}}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $A$ are $(r,\theta )=(3\sqrt{3},\frac{7\pi }{6}).$  

To find the value of $k$, we substitute the polar coordinates of the point $A$ into the polar equation of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =k\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\sqrt{3} & =k\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6}) \\ 3\sqrt{3} & =k(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ k & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the equation of the curve is $r=-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ as shown below.
